speakers.name: Priya Nair
speakers.background: Priya is a postdoctoral researcher in machine learning with four years of experience developing and evaluating clinical prediction systems from electronic health record data. Her work uses supervised learning, calibration analysis, subgroup performance audits, feature provenance checks, and interpretable-modeling tools. She has collaborated with health systems on translating model outputs into staff-facing interfaces.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Priya treats the risk score as a predictive system whose usefulness depends on valid targets, clean feature construction, reliable calibration, and performance that does not degrade across patient subgroups. She is attentive to feature leakage and to the practical question of how a ranked score can be explained clearly enough for outreach staff to use it appropriately.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

speakers.name: Dr. Elena Morales
speakers.background: Elena is a postdoctoral epidemiologist with five years of applied research experience in health-care access, preventive outreach, and observational studies using linked clinic and claims data. She designs cohort definitions, assesses selection bias and transportability, and conducts external validation studies across patient populations and care settings.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Elena frames the pilot around the epidemiologic validity of the outreach outcome and the population to which the model is meant to apply. She focuses on whether patients who appear in the data differ systematically from those who do not enter care, whether the outcome corresponds to a meaningful outreach objective, and whether validation in a new clinic population supports use beyond the development sample.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

speakers.name: Marcus Lee
speakers.background: Marcus is a postdoctoral sociologist with three years of experience studying organizational decision-making in community health settings. He uses ethnographic observation, semi-structured interviews, document analysis, and workflow mapping to examine how staff interpret data systems, distribute responsibility, and negotiate discretion in daily practice.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Marcus examines the score as something that will enter an existing workplace rather than simply produce a technical recommendation. He is concerned with how outreach staff actually incorporate or override ranked lists, who becomes accountable for those choices, and how patients may understand or respond to being sorted by a risk-based system. He favors observing the pilot in practice before assuming that formal procedures reflect real workflow.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

transcript.speaker: Marcus Lee
transcript.text: I was looking at the pilot checklist on page two, and it still treats using the ranked list like it's pretty straightforward. Before we lock that down, I'd like us to talk about what evidence we need on the model in this clinic, but also what we need to see about how staff actually work with it day to day, because—

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: On the evidence side, I’m a little worried about assuming the historical target transfers cleanly. Elena, what exactly are we calling the outreach outcome here, successful contact, an appointment completed, something else, and does it mean the same thing at this clinic? My held-out run kept discrimination, but it was overpredicting for sparse-history patients, so I don’t think a rank order alone is enough.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: I think we should leave the outcome open for the moment. Successful contact, completed appointment, and subsequent care are different estimands, and I need to confirm which of those are captured reliably here, especially since the linked review showed some apparently inactive patients with claims outside the network. Priya, could you separate the sparse-history group in the clinic data and show, show calibration there, rather than only in the held-out development set?

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: I can do that, but I’d want to freeze a genuinely pre-pilot slice before staff start seeing the queue. Otherwise the intervention changes both documentation and the outcome. I’ll stratify calibration by sparse history in the clinic extract, and I need to recheck the feature timestamps too. Especially whether any post-outreach note fields are getting, um, pulled forward.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Lee
transcript.text: That makes sense. I’d also want to know whether the clinic’s records distinguish somebody who was unreachable from somebody staff decided not to call, or somebody who declined. Otherwise the queue will make those look like the same kind of outcome. And once staff see it, their notes may change too, so the observation needs to- needs to sit alongside that pre-pilot slice.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: I would not collapse those categories in the evaluation. If a patient receives care elsewhere, or staff judge that outreach is inappropriate, that is not, not evidence the score failed in the same way as an unsuccessful call. Marcus, do those decisions usually leave a structured trace anywhere, or are we mostly relying on free-text notes?

transcript.speaker: Marcus Lee
transcript.text: Mostly free text, I think, plus occasional shorthand in the call log, but I need to verify that with the clinic. In the shadowing I have done, staff were making those distinctions from memory, language needs, and prior notes, then reordering the list without recording why, so a structured field may not, um, capture the whole story anyway.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: That's exactly the concern. If the reasons for reordering or withholding a call stay mostly informal, then the observed outcome is partly a record of staff triage, not just patient responsiveness. I think we need at least a brief prospective reason capture during the pilot, though I'd like to see- I'd like to know what fields the clinic can realistically support before we specify it.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: And from the model side, that reason capture is not just implementation detail. It changes what label we can claim to be validating. Could it be a very small set of mutually exclusive codes, plus optional text, so we can distinguish unreachable from— so, deferred by staff, without asking them to narrate every reorder?

transcript.speaker: Marcus Lee
transcript.text: I'd be cautious about making the codes too neat before we see the work. “Deferred by staff” could mean language matching, a safety concern, someone known to be in hospital, or just that there was no time that afternoon. Those carry- those have pretty different implications. Could we pilot a small set, but also observe a few huddles and calls alongside it, so we can see what gets lost in the coding?

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: I think that’s workable, as long as we don’t later treat the codes as ground truth. For the model evaluation, I’d keep the raw disposition, the optional text, and maybe a separate flag for a staff override. Then we can see whether the sparse-history calibration problem is also, also concentrated among patients being deferred for particular reasons.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: I would be careful not to make the override flag just another predictor of poor response, because it may be marking who is visible to staff as difficult to reach, rather than anything intrinsic to the patient. But yes, if we preserve the raw disposition and the text, we can estimate how much of the apparent clinic-specific performance is really selection into contact. The outside-network, the outside-network claims make that especially important.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: Mm, agreed, the override should stay out of the feature set and out of anything that sounds causal. I'd treat it as an audit variable. Among patients staff override, what were the stated reasons, and how does that intersect with sparse history and calibration? But we should define the extraction cutoff now, because even a disposition entered after the call can quietly become, uh, leakage if it lands in the EHR feed.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Lee
transcript.text: I agree on fixing the cutoff. But I’d separate that technical cutoff from when staff record an override, because in practice they may only articulate the reason after a huddle or after a failed call. Priya, what will they actually see about why the model ranked someone highly? I worry that a very terse explanation can still be read as more, um, definitive than it is.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: I’d keep it deliberately non-diagnostic. A short “why this patient is near the top” panel with the few pre-cutoff factors that contributed, and an explicit note that it’s a prioritization aid and staff judgment can override it. But I don’t want to show a pseudo-precise probability if calibration is off for sparse histories. Maybe for the pilot, it’s a ranked tier plus uncertainty language until we’ve checked clinic calibration.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: Tiering makes sense for the pilot, but the uncertainty language shouldn't- it can't obscure the population issue. For patients with little prior clinic history, we may be uncertain because they're new or disconnected from care here, or because they're getting care elsewhere, and those aren't interchangeable. Could the pre-pilot evaluation tabulate outside-network claims, where available, alongside the sparse-history strata?

transcript.speaker: Marcus Lee
transcript.text: Mm, yes, that distinction matters.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: I can add that cross-tab, with the caveat that claims availability itself may be selective. So I’d label missing claims separately rather than treat it as no outside care. What I’d really want to see is whether the overprediction persists within sparse-history patients who do and don’t have observed outside-network use. That would tell us a bit more about whether this is cohort shift versus a feature- construction problem.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: I would not expect that cross-tab by itself to separate those explanations. Observed outside-network use is only a proxy, and the missing-claims group may be selected in a different, different way again. Could we also report the size and basic composition of each cell? If some strata are very small, I would treat the calibration estimates as descriptive, rather than evidence that transportability is resolved.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: I’ll report denominators and composition for every cell, and use intervals rather than pretending the small strata settle anything. If the clinic slice is too thin for reliable calibration estimates, that itself argues against putting a calibrated risk meaning on the tiers yet. We can still assess the ranking, but, sorry, I lost my point there. We should label it as provisional.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: And if that is the result, I would not frame the pilot as validation of a transportable risk score at all. We can still learn whether a ranked, provisional queue fits the workflow, but we need to keep the clinic evaluation population explicit, explicit about who had observable records, who had claims linkage, and who was actually eligible for contact.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: That’s the right boundary. I’ll make the pre-pilot report explicit about the analytic cohort and the observability filters, and then keep the pilot interface to provisional priority tiers instead of implying a validated probability. The one thing I’d like us to settle before we close is the extraction cutoff, because I need that locked before I rerun the provenance audit.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: Before we fix the cutoff, I want it tied to the last point when all the predictors would have been available, not just the export date. And the cohort definition should keep patients excluded for insufficient observable history as a documented group. Otherwise, we will quietly make the clinic population look more stable than it really is.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: The operational definition is the cutoff at the last timestamp the live scoring pipeline could actually have seen. The export date is irrelevant, except for reproducibility. I'll retain the insufficient-history exclusions as an explicit row in the cohort flow and provenance audit, rather than silently dropping them. I just need the clinic to confirm the relevant feed-latency rules before I freeze it.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Lee
transcript.text: I think we should stop there, since we're at time. The rest can wait until the next meeting, uh, thanks, everyone.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: All right, goodbye.

speakers.name: Dr. Hannah Ortiz
speakers.background: Dr. Ortiz is a cognitive neuroscientist with 9 years of experience designing visual working-memory experiments and building fMRI task pipelines. Her work combines delayed-estimation paradigms, psychophysical analysis of precision and swap errors, and multivariate fMRI decoding of feature-specific delay-period activity. In the lab she is responsible for translating theoretical questions into trial timing, counterbalancing, acquisition constraints, and preregistered behavioral and neural outcome measures.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Ortiz treats the task and measurement design as the decisive link between claims about memory and evidence. She focuses on whether the orientation-report distribution can distinguish reduced precision from binding failures, whether delay lengths isolate maintenance rather than encoding or response processes, and whether the fMRI design has enough temporal and trial-level structure to support interpretable decoding of delay-period representations.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

speakers.name: Dr. Wei Chen
speakers.background: Dr. Chen is a computational neuroscientist with 11 years of experience fitting generative models of working-memory behavior and relating their latent variables to neural population codes. He works with circular error distributions, hierarchical Bayesian model comparison, attractor-network models, and forward models that predict how orientation information should evolve in decoded neural signals. He has collaborated extensively with experimental fMRI groups but primarily contributes model specification, identifiability checks, and simulation-based power analyses.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Chen frames the behavioral and fMRI results as joint constraints on candidate mechanisms. He asks whether a population code with drift, diffusion, or attractor dynamics produces the observed mixture of precision loss and structured errors, and whether each model makes separable predictions for changes in decoded orientation over longer delays. He is attentive to parameter recovery and to the possibility that the proposed sample may not discriminate model variants even if the behavioral effect replicates.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

transcript.speaker: Dr. Wei Chen
transcript.text: I’m looking at the task draft Hannah circulated, the one with the four delay bins. Before we get too deep into it, it’s nice that the behavior and scan task are actually the same thing. I was hoping we could pin down whether the timing gives us a clean enough delay-period signal, because then I can ask something more useful than just whether precision goes down again, or whether...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Hannah Ortiz
transcript.text: In the draft, the jittered encoding-to-delay transition is doing most of that work, but I don't want the long bins to get confounded with response preparation just because participants can anticipate the probe. I'm still checking the acquisition schedule and usable trial count. Once we know that, we can decide whether four bins really, uh, buy us more than three well-powered delays.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Wei Chen
transcript.text: Three well-separated delays may actually be better for the model comparison than four thin bins. What I’d want to know is whether, at the longest delay, we can jitter the response period independently enough that a decoded orientation change isn’t just probe anticipation. Otherwise the neural trajectory is hard to interpret, and I’d—

transcript.speaker: Dr. Hannah Ortiz
transcript.text: I think we can do that, but the report cue has to be independently jittered after every delay. It can't just come at a predictable endpoint. Otherwise, especially at twelve seconds, yeah, people can start selecting a motor plan or reactivating the likely feature. And Wei, for your fits, what would count as attractor dynamics in the circular-error distribution rather than just ordinary diffusion?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Wei Chen
transcript.text: I’d look for structure that diffusion alone doesn’t naturally give us. Errors getting increasingly pulled toward a few stable orientations, or a delay-dependent pattern of local bias along with the widening. And in the neural data, the stronger version would be decoded orientation moving toward those same states over the delay, instead of just getting noisier. But I should be careful. Aggregate precision can look almost identical under both models, so I need to run recovery with the actual trial counts before claiming we can separate them.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Hannah Ortiz
transcript.text: And that means we shouldn't treat the pilot's apparent swap increase as evidence for the attractors by itself. It was pretty concentrated in a subset of people, so I'd want the mixture model to estimate target precision, swap rate, and any local bias separately at each delay. We shouldn't let a few participants' binding failures- we shouldn't let that masquerade as a population-level drift effect.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Wei Chen
transcript.text: I agree, we should give swaps their own component instead of asking the drift term to absorb them. The tricky part is, is that with one item, a true swap is hard to define. So are you imagining multi-item trials in the same task, or is “swap-like” really a response-layout or categorical-report error from the pilot? That changes the generative model quite, quite a lot.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Hannah Ortiz
transcript.text: The pilot had two encoded orientations, and then after the delay a cue told them which location to report, so those were genuine non-target reports, though I agree the response wheel may have amplified them. For this follow-up, I'd keep the two-item display. With a single item, the precision result would be cleaner, but we'd lose the binding question, and then we shouldn't- we shouldn't call anything a swap.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Wei Chen
transcript.text: The two-item version is the right test, I think, but the model needs to keep non-target reports explicitly separate from gradual target drift. Could we randomize the response wheel across trials, or at least decouple it from the encoded locations? If that layout is contributing, we might otherwise interpret a really mundane motor or display bias as a delay-dependent binding- as a delay-dependent binding effect.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Hannah Ortiz
transcript.text: I'd randomize the wheel's reference orientation trial by trial and keep it spatially neutral relative to the two encoded locations. I don't think that fully removes response-selection effects, though, so I'd also counterbalance the probe location and model any systematic report bias before we, we call a non-target response a binding failure. The twelve-second condition is where that could get ugly.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Wei Chen
transcript.text: And if the twelve-second trials have a stronger generic response bias, the mixture could still label some of that as swaps unless we put the bias in the observation model. I'd like to simulate the randomized wheel and probe-location counterbalancing explicitly, mostly to see whether the model can recover a real delay effect in, in swap rate separately from that nuisance pattern.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Hannah Ortiz
transcript.text: But I’d separate two questions in the simulations. One is recovery of the swap parameter under the randomized wheel, and the other is whether we have enough trials per participant to estimate it at twelve seconds at all. If that subset pattern from the pilot is real, pooling people could make a fairly bad individual-level estimate look like a clean, clean delay effect.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Wei Chen
transcript.text: Hierarchical fitting may help us borrow strength across people without pretending everyone has the same swap rate, but it won't manufacture information for the long-delay condition. I'd want to simulate a subgroup with genuinely elevated swaps and ask whether the model recovers that heterogeneity. Or whether it- whether it shrinks that into a misleading group-level delay slope.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Hannah Ortiz
transcript.text: And I don't want hierarchical shrinkage to be the reason we call the pilot subgroup a graded maintenance effect. Could your recovery grid include, like, a sparse high-swap subgroup with no true delay slope, and then, then the converse, a uniform small slope across everybody? If we can't distinguish those at the usable long-delay trial count, we may need to treat swaps as exploratory rather than a co-primary outcome.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Wei Chen
transcript.text: That’s the right grid. I’d include those two cases, and also a condition where response bias goes up only at twelve seconds, because that’s the failure mode I’m most worried about.
